semantic_correction.stem: A postpartum client develops a new abnormal vital-sign pattern that meets the hospital’s maternal early-warning trigger. Which nursing action best reflects the purpose of the early-warning system?

options.A: Treat the trigger as a signal for possible deterioration: follow the facility MEWS protocol now, escalate as indicated, and continue focused assessment.
options.B: Use the trigger to identify the most likely obstetric diagnosis, begin diagnosis-specific treatment, and reassess the client after the first intervention.
options.C: Repeat the abnormal vital signs at the next routine assessment before escalating, because a postpartum trigger may reflect expected physiologic recovery.
options.D: Escalate the abnormal findings, then pause further bedside assessment until the responding clinician determines which maternal condition is present.

semantic_correction.rationale: The current Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health Maternal Early Warning System Implementation Resource Kit describes MEWS as a system for early recognition of changes in pregnant and postpartum patients' vital signs and clinical conditions that leads to effective escalation and prompt evaluation. Its trigger criteria example directs the team to validate the trigger, notify the responding provider, activate the escalation process, and then continue provider evaluation and differential diagnosis. The example protocol also requires monitoring, reevaluation, diagnostic or therapeutic interventions, and further escalation when needed. Live ACOG guidance independently states that early-warning triggers mandate further action according to protocol and that the protocol should provide for a full evaluation of the problem. Therefore A is correct. B converts a warning trigger into a specific diagnosis before evaluation. C delays a protocol-triggered response despite a new postpartum abnormal pattern. D appropriately escalates but then incorrectly stops the bedside assessment and monitoring that should continue while the cause is evaluated.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Use maternal early-warning triggers as signals of possible deterioration that require timely protocol-based reassessment and escalation while continuing clinical assessment to determine the cause.
semantic_correction.source_organization: Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health (AIM) / American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)

semantic_correction.source_version_date: Current AIM MEWS resource-kit webpage and PDF rechecked August 20, 2026; PDF is served from a 2025 resource path and includes an example protocol dated November 2023. Live ACOG Committee Opinion No. 590 page rechecked August 20, 2026.
semantic_correction.source_locator: AIM MEWS Resource Kit Introduction, PDF p.3 / pageno 2: MEWS supports early recognition of changes in pregnant and postpartum patients leading to effective escalation and prompt evaluation. Recognition and Prevention, PDF p.9–10 / pageno 8–9: facilities identify trigger vital signs/symptoms, responding provider, notification process, response time, and standardized escalation plan; trigger example proceeds from Trigger MEWS to provider notification, escalation, provider evaluation, and differential diagnosis. Appendix C, PDF p.24–26 / pageno 23–25: immediate action when criteria are triggered per facility protocol, bedside evaluation, monitoring/re-evaluation, diagnostic/therapeutic interventions, huddle, and further escalation if triggers persist. ACOG Early Warning Systems in the Inpatient Setting: triggers mandate further actions according to protocol and the protocol should provide for a full evaluation of the problem.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: A maternal early-warning trigger is a recognition-and-escalation signal for possible deterioration in pregnant or postpartum patients; it prompts timely protocol-based notification, evaluation, reassessment, and escalation rather than establishing a diagnosis or replacing ongoing bedside assessment.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup retained the maternal early-warning escalation construct, replaced the old absolute/length-cued distractors with plausible competing responses, strengthened currentness with the current AIM MEWS implementation resource kit, and preserved the distinction between a warning trigger and a diagnosis.

scope_exclusions.specific_trigger_threshold: The item does not test a universal numeric MEWS cutoff; trigger criteria are facility/protocol dependent and the stem states that the local trigger has already been met.
scope_exclusions.specific_diagnosis: No diagnosis such as hemorrhage, preeclampsia, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, or cardiomyopathy is established by the trigger itself.
scope_exclusions.specific_treatment: The item does not direct diagnosis-specific medication or procedural treatment before evaluation establishes the clinical problem.
scope_exclusions.postpartum_scope: The current AIM MEWS resource explicitly includes postpartum patients and postpartum settings of care; the item does not limit MEWS to antepartum or intrapartum care.
scope_exclusions.clinical_judgment: The early-warning system complements rather than replaces nursing assessment, monitoring, and clinical judgment.
scope_exclusions.facility_protocol: Exact notification chains, response-time targets, and standing orders vary by facility; the tested principle is prompt protocol-based response once a local trigger is met.

near_duplicate_check.note: Targeted GitHub search for ‘maternal early warning postpartum trigger escalation prompt evaluation diagnosis’ returned no indexed repository match. No broad bank scan was performed.

option_audit.A: Correct. It treats the trigger as possible deterioration, activates the local response promptly, and preserves ongoing assessment while the cause is determined.
option_audit.B: Plausible because warning criteria can point toward serious obstetric disease, but a trigger is not diagnostic and does not justify choosing diagnosis-specific treatment without evaluation.
option_audit.C: Plausible because abnormal postpartum findings sometimes require confirmation, but the stem states that the hospital trigger is met; routine-delay logic conflicts with the purpose of prompt escalation.
option_audit.D: Plausible because escalation brings additional expertise, but bedside assessment and monitoring should continue rather than stop while the responding clinician evaluates the cause.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. A alone combines prompt protocol response with continued assessment. B overdiagnoses, C delays a trigger-defined response, and D abandons ongoing bedside assessment after escalation.

cueing_check.note: The key is not longest. All four alternatives are parallel nursing responses of nearly identical length. The word ‘trigger’ appears across A/B/C rather than uniquely cueing the key, and no only/all/always/never/every pattern is used.
